notes.meaning: Jesus enters the synagogue at Capernaum on the Sabbath day. A man is there whose hand is withered and paralyzed, leaving him unable to work for his living. Even with this disability, the man still comes to the place of worship, where Jesus meets him.

The religious leaders watch Jesus closely to see if He will heal on the Sabbath. They do not care about the man's suffering, but only want an excuse to accuse Jesus of breaking their rules. By watching to see if He will heal, they show they already know He has God's power.

Jesus tells the man with the withered hand to step into the middle of the room where everyone can see him. He does not hide what He is about to do. By bringing the man forward, Jesus invites the crowd to feel pity and shows He will not be intimidated by His critics.

Jesus asks the leaders whether Sabbath law allows people to do good or do evil, to save life or to kill. Refusing to help someone when you have the power to do so is like doing harm. The critics stay completely silent because they are secretly plotting to kill Jesus while He is working to heal.

Jesus looks around at the leaders with anger and deep sorrow at how stubborn and uncaring their hearts are. He tells the man to stretch out his hand, and as the man obeys, his hand is completely healed. Jesus shows that godly anger is directed against sin while still caring for the sinner.

The Pharisees leave the synagogue and quickly meet with the Herodians, a political group that backed King Herod. Even though these two groups normally dislike each other, their shared hatred of Jesus brings them together. They immediately begin plotting a way to have Jesus put to death.

Jesus withdraws to the Sea of Galilee with His disciples to step away from the plot against His life. Enormous crowds follow Him from Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, and even Gentile regions like Tyre and Sidon. People travel great distances because they hear about the wonderful things He is doing.

Jesus tells His disciples to keep a small fishing boat ready by the shore. The crowd is so large and eager that people are pressing in on Him from every side. Having the boat ready gives Him a place to step back and teach safely without being crushed.

Jesus cures many sick people, which makes everyone with painful diseases rush forward to touch Him. They believe that even physical contact with Him will make them well. In their deep suffering, they eagerly run to Jesus as their true healer.

Whenever evil spirits see Jesus, they fall down before Him and scream that He is the Son of God. Jesus strictly orders them to be quiet and not make Him known. He refuses to take praise or testimony from demons, and the proper time to reveal His identity has not yet arrived.

Jesus goes up a mountain and calls the specific followers He wants to join Him. They leave the crowd behind and come directly to Him. Jesus spent the whole night in prayer before choosing them, showing that church leaders should always be chosen with prayer.

Jesus chooses twelve men to be His apostles, which means messengers sent on a mission. Their first task is simply to live with Him and learn from Him so they can be trained. Then He sends them out to preach the gospel and gives them power to cast out demons.

First on the list is Simon, whom Jesus names Peter, meaning a rock. Then come James and John, the sons of Zebedee, whom Jesus nicknames the Sons of Thunder. This name describes their fiery, energetic temperaments and the bold power with which they would preach.

The rest of the twelve are Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot. This group includes former political enemies, such as Matthew the tax collector for Rome and Simon who opposed Rome. Judas is named last as the one who would betray Jesus, an appointment Jesus allowed in order to fulfill God's plan.

Jesus and His disciples go into a house, and another large crowd gathers right away. The needy crowd is so dense and demanding that Jesus and the disciples do not even have time to eat bread. Jesus gladly sets aside His own food and comfort to serve the people.

When Jesus' family hears about the crowds and how He is missing meals, they set out to take charge of Him. They say He is out of His mind and acting like someone who has lost His senses. Even His own family struggles to understand His great zeal for God's work.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some early manuscripts change this verse so that the scribes say Jesus is mad, likely to avoid embarrassing the family, but the original text shows Jesus' family genuinely misjudged Him.

notes.meaning: Teachers of the law travel down from Jerusalem to discredit Jesus' ministry. Unable to deny that He drives out demons, they claim He is possessed by Beelzebul, the prince of demons. They try to convince the crowd that Jesus gets His power from the devil rather than from God.

Jesus calls His critics to Himself and answers them using parables, which are short word pictures that teach a deeper truth. He asks them how Satan can drive out Satan. This simple question exposes how senseless their accusation really is.
Jesus points out that a nation torn apart by civil war cannot survive. In the same way, a household fighting against itself will quickly fall. Internal conflict always brings ruin to any group.

If Satan were fighting his own demons and tearing down his own evil work, his power would come to an end. Satan is wicked, but he is not foolish enough to destroy his own kingdom. The scribes' claim therefore makes no sense.

Jesus pictures Satan as a strong man guarding his house. No one can steal the strong man's property unless he first ties him up. By rescuing people from demonic control, Jesus proves He is stronger than Satan and is breaking his power.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern spiritual warfare teachings use this passage to claim believers have authority to bind territorial spirits over cities, though the text is about Christ's victory over Satan.

notes.meaning: Jesus gives a solemn promise that human beings can be forgiven for all kinds of sins and offensive speech. God's mercy is wide enough to wash away even terrible failures when people turn to Him. This gives great comfort to anyone who worries they have sinned too much.

Jesus warns that whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven and is guilty of an eternal sin. This means becoming so hardened against the Spirit's clear witness that a person refuses to repent. Because forgiveness comes only through repentance, rejecting the Spirit cuts a person off from the cure.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Early church fathers like Augustine explained blasphemy against the Holy Spirit as final impenitence, which means stubbornly refusing to repent of sin up to the moment of death.

notes.meaning: Mark explains why Jesus gave this strict warning. The scribes were looking directly at miracles done by the Holy Spirit and claiming they came from an evil spirit. Calling God's holy work demonic showed their hearts were in grave danger.

Jesus' mother and brothers arrive, but they cannot get through the dense crowd, so they wait outside. They send a message into the house asking for Jesus. People sitting in the circle pass the word to Jesus that His family is outside asking for Him.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Catholic and Orthodox traditions hold that Mary remained a virgin throughout her life, interpreting these brothers as Joseph's sons from a prior marriage or as cousins.

notes.meaning: Jesus answers the message by asking who His mother and brothers really are. He does not say this to disrespect His earthly family, but to point to a higher spiritual family. He uses the moment to teach what it really means to belong to Him.

Jesus looks around at the circle of people sitting at His feet and calls them His mother and brothers. He declares that whoever does the will of God belongs to His true family. Loving obedience to God creates a bond with Christ that is even deeper than physical blood ties.
